documentNotes.title: Full native editorial preface
documentNotes.statement:
Preface This publication contains 39 theoretical and 14 practical competition problems from the 41st – 45th International Chemistry Olympiads (IChO) organized in the years 2009 – 2013. It has been published by the IChO International Information Centre in Bratislava (Slovakia) as a continuation of the preceding Volumes 1 and 2 published on the occasion of the 40th anniversary of the IChO with the titles: • The competition problems from the International Chemistry Olympiads, Volume 1, 1st – 20th IChO, 1968 – 1988 (IUVENTA, Bratislava, 2008). • The competition problems from the International Chemistry Olympiads, Volume 2, 21st – 40th IChO, 1989 – 2008 (IUVENTA, Bratislava, 2009). Not less than 318 theoretical and 110 practical problems were set in the IChO during the forty-five years of its existence. In the elaboration of this collection the editor had to face certain difficulties because the aim was not only to make use of past recordings but also to give them such a form that they may be used in practice and further chemical education. Consequently, it was necessary to make some corrections in order to unify the form of the problems (numbering the tasks of the particular problems, solution inserted immediately after the text of the problem, solutions without grading points and special graphs used for grading of practical problems). Nevertheless, the mentioned corrections and changes do not concern the contents and language of the competition problems. The practical problems set in the IChO competitions, contain as a rule some instructions, list of apparatuses available, chemicals on each desk and those available in the laboratory, and the risk and safety phrases with regard to the chemicals used. All of these items are important for the competitors during the competition but less important for those who are going to read the competition tasks of this collection and thus, they are omitted. Some parts of the solutions of practical problems are also left out since they require the experimental data which could be obtained by experiments during the practical part of the IChO competition. In this publication SI quantities and units are preferred. Only some exceptions have been made when, in an effort to preserve the original text, the quantities and units have been used that are not SI. Although the numbers of significant figures in the results of some solutions do not obey the criteria generally accepted, they were left without change.

Unfortunately, the authors of the particular competition problems are not known and due to the procedure of creation of the IChO competition problems, it is impossible to assign any author's name to a particular problem. Nevertheless, responsibility for the scientific content and language of the problems lies exclusively with the organizers of the particular International Chemistry Olympiads. This review of the competition problems from the 41st – 45th IChO should serve to both competitors and their teachers as a source of further ideas in their preparation for this difficult competition. For those who have taken part in some of these International Chemistry Olympiads the collection of the problems could be of help as archival and documentary material. In the previous forty-five years many known and unknown people - teachers, authors, pupils, and organizers proved their abilities and knowledge and contributed to the success of this already well known and world-wide competition. We wish to all who will organize and attend the future International Chemistry Olympiads, success and happiness. Bratislava, July 2014 Anton Sirota, editor

Source note: This Ankara2011 section prints practical chemical lists, procedures, reference tables/graphs and native evaluation conditions, all retained. Referenced but absent answer sheets, distribution graphs, original points and competitor-dependent results are not invented.

problems.title: Theoretical problem 1 — Nitrogen oxide reaction kinetics
problems.statement:
Nitrogen oxides, common pollutants in the ambient air, are primarily nitric oxide, NO, and nitrogen dioxide, NO₂. Atmospheric nitric oxide is produced mainly during thunderstorms and in the internal combustion engines. At high temperatures NO reacts with H₂ to produce nitrous oxide, N₂O, a greenhouse gas.

$$2\,\mathrm{NO}(g)+\mathrm{H_2}(g)\to\mathrm{N_2O}(g)+\mathrm{H_2O}(g).$$

To study the kinetics of this reaction at 820 °C, initial rates for the formation of N₂O were measured using various initial partial pressures of NO and H₂.

| Experiment | Initial p(NO) / torr | Initial p(H₂) / torr | Initial rate of N₂O production / torr s⁻¹ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 120.0 | 60.0 | 8.66·10⁻² |
| 2 | 60.0 | 60.0 | 2.17·10⁻² |
| 3 | 60.0 | 180.0 | 6.62·10⁻² |

Throughout this problem do not use concentrations. Use units of pressure (torr) and time in seconds.

parts.statement: Determine the experimental rate law and calculate the rate constant.

Calculate the initial rate of disappearance of NO, if NO with a pressure of 2.00·10² torr and H₂ with 1.00·10² torr are mixed at 820 °C. (If you have been unable to calculate the value for the rate constant, you can use the value of 2·10⁻⁷ in appropriate unit.)

Calculate the time elapsed to reduce the partial pressure of H₂ to the half of its initial value, if NO with a pressure of 8.00·10² torr and H₂ with 1.0 torr are mixed at 820 °C. (If you have been unable to calculate the value for the rate constant, you can use the value of 2·10⁻⁷ in appropriate unit.)
parts.statementAfter:
A proposed mechanism for the reaction between NO and H₂ is given below:

$$2\,\mathrm{NO}(g)\underset{k_{-1}}{\stackrel{k_1}{\rightleftharpoons}}\mathrm{N_2O_2}(g),\qquad\mathrm{N_2O_2}(g)+\mathrm{H_2}(g)\xrightarrow{k_2}\mathrm{N_2O}(g)+\mathrm{H_2O}(g).$$

parts.statement: Derive the rate law for the formation of N₂O from the proposed mechanism using the steady-state approximation for the intermediate.

Under what condition does this rate law reduce to the experimentally determined rate law found in Part 1.1? Tick the relevant answer.

- If $k_{-1}\ll k_2p_{\mathrm{H_2}}$.
- If $k_{-1}\gg k_2p_{\mathrm{H_2}}$.
- If $k_{-1}>k_2$.
- If $k_1>k_{-1}$.
Express the experimentally determined rate constant $k$ in terms of $k_1$, $k_{-1}$ and $k_2$.

Select the schematic energy diagram that is consistent with the proposed reaction mechanism and experimental rate law.

[figure: p1-fig1]

[figure: p1-fig2]

figures.alt: Native energy diagrams a–c, full energy/reaction-coordinate axes, arrowheads and letter labels.
Native energy diagrams d–f, full energy/reaction-coordinate axes, arrowheads and letter labels.

solution.statement:
**1.1**

$$R=k(p_{\mathrm{NO}})^a(p_{\mathrm{H_2}})^b.$$

$$\frac{R_1}{R_2}=\frac{8.66\cdot10^{-2}}{2.17\cdot10^{-2}}=3.99=\frac{k120^a60^b}{k60^a60^b}=2^a=3.99\Rightarrow a=2.$$

$$\frac{R_3}{R_2}=\frac{6.62\cdot10^{-2}}{2.17\cdot10^{-2}}=3.05=\frac{k60^a180^b}{k60^a60^b}=3^b=3.05\Rightarrow b=1.$$

$$R=k(p_{\mathrm{NO}})^2p_{\mathrm{H_2}},\qquad k=\frac{8.66\cdot10^{-2}}{120^2\times60}=1.00\cdot10^{-7}\,\mathrm{torr^{-2}\,s^{-1}}.$$

**1.2**

$$R=\frac{\Delta p_{\mathrm{N_2O}}}{\Delta t}=-\frac12\frac{\Delta p_{\mathrm{NO}}}{\Delta t}=1.0\cdot10^{-7}\times200^2\times100=0.40\,\mathrm{torr\,s^{-1}}.$$

$$-\frac{\Delta p_{\mathrm{NO}}}{\Delta t}=0.80\,\mathrm{torr\,s^{-1}}.$$

**1.3** $R=k(p_{\mathrm{NO}})^2p_{\mathrm{H_2}}$. Since $p_{\mathrm{NO}}\gg p_{\mathrm{H_2}}$, $R=k'p_{\mathrm{H_2}}$, where $k'=k(p_{\mathrm{NO}})^2$.

$$k'=1.0\cdot10^{-7}(8.00\cdot10^2)^2=0.064\,\mathrm{s^{-1}},\qquad t_{1/2}=\frac{\ln2}{k'}=10.8\,\mathrm s.$$

**1.4**

$$\frac{\Delta p_{\mathrm{N_2O}}}{\Delta t}=k_2p_{\mathrm{N_2O_2}}p_{\mathrm{H_2}}.$$

Steady-state approximation for N₂O₂:

$$\frac{\Delta p_{\mathrm{N_2O_2}}}{\Delta t}=0=k_1(p_{\mathrm{NO}})^2-k_{-1}p_{\mathrm{N_2O_2}}-k_2p_{\mathrm{N_2O_2}}p_{\mathrm{H_2}}=0.$$

$$p_{\mathrm{N_2O_2}}=\frac{k_1(p_{\mathrm{NO}})^2}{k_{-1}+k_2p_{\mathrm{H_2}}},\quad\frac{\Delta p_{\mathrm{N_2O}}}{\Delta t}=k_2p_{\mathrm{H_2}}\frac{k_1(p_{\mathrm{NO}})^2}{k_{-1}+k_2p_{\mathrm{H_2}}}.$$

$$R=k_1k_2\frac{(p_{\mathrm{NO}})^2p_{\mathrm{H_2}}}{k_{-1}+k_2p_{\mathrm{H_2}}}.$$

**1.5** Correct answer: if $k_{-1}\gg k_2p_{\mathrm{H_2}}$.

**1.6** $k=k_1k_2/k_{-1}$.

**1.7** Energy diagram d is correct.

problems.title: Theoretical problem 2 — Ammonia combustion and titration
problems.statement:
Anhydrous ammonia is an ultra-clean, energy-dense alternative liquid fuel. It produces no greenhouse gases on combustion. In an experiment, gaseous NH₃ is burned with O₂ in a container of fixed volume according to the equation:

$$4\,\mathrm{NH_3}(g)+3\,\mathrm{O_2}(g)\to2\,\mathrm{N_2}(g)+6\,\mathrm{H_2O}(l).$$

The initial and final states are at 298 K. After combustion with 14.40 g of O₂, some of NH₃ remains unreacted.

parts.statement: Calculate the heat released during the process. ΔfH°(NH₃(g)) = −46.11 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔfH°(H₂O(l)) = −285.83 kJ mol⁻¹.
parts.statementAfter: To determine the amount of NH₃ gas dissolved in water, produced during the combustion process, a 10.00 cm³ sample of the aqueous solution was withdrawn from the reaction vessel and added to 15.0 cm³ of a H₂SO₄ solution (c = 0.0100 mol dm⁻³). The resulting solution was titrated with a standard NaOH solution (c = 0.0200 mol dm⁻³) and the equivalence point was reached at 10.64 cm³. Kb(NH₃) = 1.8·10⁻⁵; Ka(HSO₄⁻) = 1.1·10⁻².

parts.statement: Calculate pH of the solution in the container after combustion.

At the end point of titration, NH₄⁺ and SO₄²⁻ ions are present in the solution. Write the equations for the relevant equilibria to show how the presence of these two ions affects the pH and calculate their equilibrium constant(s).
Tick the correct statement for the pH of the solution at the equivalence point: pH > 7; pH = 7; pH < 7.

solution.statement:
**2.1** $q_v=\Delta E=\Delta H-\Delta n_gRT$. For 1 mole of NH₃:

$$\Delta H=\frac32(-285.83)-(-46.11)=-382.64\,\mathrm{kJ},\qquad\Delta n_g=-1.25\,\mathrm{mol}.$$

$$\Delta E=-382.64\,\mathrm{kJ}-[(-1.25\,\mathrm{mol})\times8.314\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}\times298\,\mathrm K]=-379.5\,\mathrm{kJ}.$$

$$n(\mathrm{O_2})=\frac{14.4\,\mathrm g}{32.0\,\mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}}=0.450\,\mathrm{mol},\quad n(\mathrm{NH_3})_{\rm reacted}=0.450\times\frac43=0.600\,\mathrm{mol}.$$

$$q_v=\Delta E=0.600\,\mathrm{mol}\times(-379.5\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}})=-227.7\,\mathrm{kJ}.$$

**2.2** Total $n(\mathrm{H_2SO_4})=15.00\,\mathrm{cm^3}\times0.0100\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}=0.150\,\mathrm{mmol}$.

H₂SO₄ + 2 NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2 H₂O. After back titration with NaOH:

$$n(\mathrm{H_2SO_4})_{\rm reacted}=\tfrac12n(\mathrm{NaOH})_{\rm reacted}=\tfrac12(0.01064\,\mathrm{dm^3}\times0.0200\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}})=1.064\cdot10^{-4}\,\mathrm{mol}=0.1064\,\mathrm{mmol}.$$

$n(\mathrm{H_2SO_4})$ reacted with NH₃ = 0.0436 mmol. 2 NH₃ + H₂SO₄ → (NH₄)₂SO₄.

$$n(\mathrm{NH_3})=2\times0.0436=0.0872\,\mathrm{mmol},\quad c(\mathrm{NH_3})=\frac{0.0872\,\mathrm{mmol}}{0.0100\,\mathrm{dm^3}}=8.72\cdot10^{-3}\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}.$$

NH₃(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ NH₄⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq), with equilibrium amounts c−x, x, x.

$$K_b=1.8\cdot10^{-5}=\frac{x^2}{0.00872-x},\quad x=[\mathrm{OH^-}]=3.96\cdot10^{-4},\quad\mathrm{pOH}=3.41,\quad\mathrm{pH}=10.59.$$

**2.3** SO₄²⁻(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ HSO₄⁻(aq) + OH⁻(aq).

$$K_b=\frac{K_w}{K_a}=\frac{1.0\cdot10^{-14}}{1.1\cdot10^{-2}}=9.1\cdot10^{-13}.$$

NH₄⁺(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ NH₃(aq) + H₃O⁺(aq).

$$K_a=\frac{K_w}{K_b}=\frac{1.0\cdot10^{-14}}{1.8\cdot10^{-5}}=5.6\cdot10^{-10}.$$

**2.4** Correct answer: pH < 7.0.

problems.title: Theoretical problem 3 — Vibrational and electronic energies
problems.statement:
At a temperature of 0 K, the total energy of a gaseous diatomic molecule AB is approximately given by $E=E_0+E_{\rm vib}$, where $E_0$ is the electronic energy of the ground state and $E_{\rm vib}$ is the vibrational energy. Allowed values of the vibrational energies are:

$$E_{\rm vib}=(\nu+\tfrac12)\varepsilon,\quad\nu=0,1,2,\ldots,\quad\varepsilon=\frac{h}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{k}{\mu}},\quad\mu(\mathrm{AB})=\frac{m_Am_B}{m_A+m_B}.$$

Here h is Planck’s constant, ν the vibrational quantum number, k the force constant and μ the reduced mass. At 0 K, ν may safely be assumed zero, and E₀ and k independent of isotopic substitution. Deuterium, D, is an isotope of hydrogen atom with mass number 2. For H₂, k = 575.11 N m⁻¹; isotopic molar masses of H and D are 1.0078 and 2.0141 g mol⁻¹. At 0 K, ε(H₂) = 1.1546 ε(HD) and ε(D₂) = 0.8167 ε(HD).

parts.statement: Calculate the enthalpy change ΔH in kJ mol⁻¹ for H₂(g) + D₂(g) → 2 HD(g) at 0 K.
Calculate the frequency in s⁻¹ of infrared photons that can be absorbed by HD molecule. (If you have been unable to calculate ε(HD), use 8.000·10⁻²⁰ J.)
parts.statementAfter: The allowed electronic energies of H atom are $E=-R_H/n^2$, $n=1,2,\ldots$, where $R_H=13.5984\,\mathrm{eV}$ and 1 eV = 1.602·10⁻¹⁹ J. The total ground-state energy of H₂ is −31.675 eV, relative to the same reference as that of hydrogen atom.

parts.statement: Calculate the dissociation energy DE in eV of a ground-state hydrogen molecule such that both H atoms are produced in their ground states.

A molecule H₂ in the ground state dissociates into its atoms after absorbing a photon of wavelength 77.0 nm. Determine all possibilities for the electronic states of hydrogen atoms produced. For each case calculate the total kinetic energy KE in eV of the dissociated hydrogen atoms.
Calculate the electron affinity EA of H₂⁺ ion in eV if its dissociation energy is 2.650 eV. (If you have been unable to calculate the dissociation energy of H₂, use 4.500 eV.)

solution.statement:
**3.1** H₂(g) + D₂(g) → 2 HD(g). $\Delta H=\Delta E+\Delta n_gRT$; $\Delta n_g=0$, so $\Delta H=\Delta E$.

$$\Delta E=2E(\mathrm{HD})-E(\mathrm{H_2})-E(\mathrm{D_2}),\quad E_{\rm vib}=\tfrac12\varepsilon\quad(\nu=0\text{ at }0\,\mathrm K).$$

$$\Delta E=2(E_0+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HD}}/2)-(E_0+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{H_2}}/2)-(E_0+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{D_2}}/2)=\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HD}}-\tfrac12(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{H_2}}+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{D_2}}).$$

$$\Delta E=\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HD}}[1-\tfrac12(1.1546+0.8167)]=0.01435\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HD}}.$$

$$\mu(\mathrm{HD})=\frac{m_Hm_D}{m_H+m_D}=\frac{(1.0078\cdot10^{-3})(2.0141\cdot10^{-3})/N_A^2}{(1.0078\cdot10^{-3}+2.0141\cdot10^{-3})/N_A}=1.1154\cdot10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg}.$$

For one HD molecule:

$$\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HD}}=\frac{h}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{k}{\mu}}=\frac{6.6261\cdot10^{-34}}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{575.11}{1.1154\cdot10^{-27}}}=7.5724\cdot10^{-20}\,\mathrm J.$$

For 1 mol of HD, the key prints:

$$\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HD}}=7.5724\cdot10^{-20}\,\mathrm J\times N_A=7.5724\cdot10^{-20}\times6.0221\cdot10^{23}=45\,600\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}.$$

$$\Delta H=\Delta E=0.01435\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HD}}=0.6544\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}.$$

Source note: The printed 45 600 kJ mol⁻¹ intermediate unit/result conflicts with the following ΔH; it is preserved as printed.

**3.2** $h\nu=\Delta E$. $\Delta E=E_{\nu1}-E_{\nu0}=(3/2-1/2)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HD}}=\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HD}}$; hence $\nu=\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HD}}/h$. From 3.1, ε(HD) = 7.5724·10⁻²⁰ J. The key prints:

$$\nu=\frac{7.5724\cdot10^{-20}\,\mathrm J}{6.6261\cdot10^{-34}\,\mathrm{J\,s}}=1.1428\cdot10^{-14}\,\mathrm s.$$

Source note: The negative exponent and unit s are native printed discrepancies; no silent correction is made.

**3.3** H₂ → 2 H; for n = 1, ΔE = 2(−13.5984) − (−31.675) = 4.478 eV.

**3.4** H₂ + hν → H + H. The key first lists (n₁,n₂) = (1,1), (1,2), (2,1), (2,2), … . H₂ ground-state energy is −31.675 eV; λ = 77.0 nm.

$$E_{\rm photon}=\frac{hc}{\lambda}=\frac{6.6261\cdot10^{-34}\times3.00\cdot10^8}{77.0\cdot10^{-9}}=2.58\cdot10^{-18}\,\mathrm J.$$

The following two expressions are printed:

$$E_{\rm photon}=\frac{6.6261\cdot10^{-34}}{1.602\cdot10^{-19}}=16.1\,\mathrm{eV},$$

$$\Delta E=E_{n1}+E_{n2}-E_{n\mathrm{H_2}}=-\frac{R_H}{n_1^2}-\frac{R_H}{n_2^2}-(31.675)<16.1\,\mathrm{eV}.$$

Source note: The eV-conversion numerator and the sign before (31.675) are printed inconsistently with the preceding and following lines. Both native expressions are preserved.

For n₁ = n₂ = 1:

$$\Delta E=-\frac{13.5984}{1^2}-\frac{13.5984}{1^2}+31.675=4.478\,\mathrm{eV},\quad\mathrm{KE}=16.1-4.478=11.6\,\mathrm{eV}.$$

For (n₁,n₂) = (1,2) or (2,1):

$$\Delta E=-\frac{13.5984}{1^2}-\frac{13.5984}{2^2}+31.675=14.677\,\mathrm{eV},\quad\mathrm{KE}=16.1-14.677=1.4\,\mathrm{eV}.$$

For n₁ = n₂ = 2:

$$\Delta E=-\frac{13.5984}{2^2}-\frac{13.5984}{2^2}+31.675=24.880\,\mathrm{eV}>16.1\,\mathrm{eV}.$$

The key then prints “K.E. = 16.1 − 14.677 = 1.4 eV” again. Source note: This is a copied expression under the forbidden case, retained explicitly. The key concludes that the possibilities are (1,1), (1,2), (2,1).

**3.5** The native ionization-potential expression prints:

$$\mathrm{IP(H)}=\Delta E_{n\to\infty}=-\frac{13.5984}{\infty^2}-\frac{13.5984}{1^2}=13.598\,\mathrm{eV}.$$

Source note: The second minus sign conflicts with the stated positive result; both are printed on native124 and retained.

| Process | Energy relation |
|---|---|
| H₂⁺ + e → H₂ | EA(H₂⁺) = −IP(H₂) |
| H₂⁺ → H⁺ + H | DE(H₂⁺) = 2.650 eV |
| H → H⁺ + e | IP(H) = 13.598 eV |
| H₂ → H + H | DE(H₂) = 4.478 eV |

$$\mathrm{EA(H_2^+)}=\mathrm{DE(H_2^+)}-\mathrm{IP(H)}-\mathrm{DE(H_2)}=2.650-13.598-4.478=-15.426\,\mathrm{eV}.$$

Electron affinity H₂⁺ = −15.426 eV.

problems.title: Theoretical problem 4 — Hydrogen generation and fuel cells
problems.statement:
For sustainable energy, hydrogen appears to be the best energy carrier. The most efficient way of using hydrogen is generation of electrical energy in a fuel cell. However, storing hydrogen in large quantities is a challenge in fuel cell applications. Among chemical hydrides considered as solid hydrogen storage materials, sodium borohydride (NaBH₄), being non-toxic, stable and environmentally benign, appears to be the most promising one. Its hydrolysis releases H₂ gas slowly at ambient temperature and needs to be catalyzed.

NaBH₄(aq) + 2 H₂O(l) → Na⁺(aq) + BO₂⁻(aq) + 4 H₂(g), with a catalyst.

Colloidal ruthenium(0) nanoclusters are the most active catalysts in this hydrolysis even at room temperature and lead to complete H₂ release. Kinetic studies show first order with respect to the catalyst but zero order with respect to the substrate. The rate of hydrogen production per mole of ruthenium is 92 mol H₂ (mol Ru)⁻¹ min⁻¹ at 25 °C.

parts.statement: Calculate the amount of ruthenium catalyst (in mg) which must be added to 0.100 dm³ of NaBH₄ solution with concentration 1.0 mol dm⁻³ to supply hydrogen at 0.100 dm³ min⁻¹ at 25 °C and 1.0 atm, as required for a portable fuel cell.
For how many minutes will this system supply hydrogen gas at this rate?
The Arrhenius activation energy is Ea = 42.0 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate the temperature required to achieve the same rate of hydrogen evolution using half the amount of ruthenium catalyst used at 25.0 °C.

A fuel cell (see figure) is made up of three segments sandwiched together: the anode, electrolyte and cathode. Hydrogen is fuel and oxygen oxidant. Two chemical reactions occur at the interfaces:

O₂(g) + 2 H₂O(l) + 4 e⁻ → 4 OH⁻(aq),

H₂(g) + 2 OH⁻(aq) → 2 H₂O(l) + 2 e⁻.

Net: 2 H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2 H₂O(l).

[figure: p4-fig1]

Hydrogen is supplied from sodium-borohydride hydrolysis. Calculate the standard cathode half-reaction potential if the anode standard reduction potential is −0.83 V and ΔfG°(H₂O(l)) is −237 kJ mol⁻¹.
Calculate the volume of air at 25 °C and 1.0 atm needed to generate a constant current of 2.5 A for 3.0 hours in this cell. Assume air contains 20% by volume O₂(g).

Fuel-cell efficiency is the ratio of work produced to heat dissipated by the cell reaction: $\eta_{\rm fuel\ cell}=\mathrm{work}/\mathrm{heat}$. Calculate the maximum efficiency at 25 °C and standard pressure using:

| Species | S° / J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ |
|---|---|
| H₂(g) | 130.7 |
| O₂(g) | 205.2 |
| H₂O(l) | 70.0 |
parts.statementAfter:
The second law of thermodynamics states that it is impossible to convert all heat qH from a high-temperature reservoir TH into work. Some energy qC must be transferred to a low-temperature reservoir TC. Thus a 100% efficient heat engine is thermodynamically impossible. Reversible operation, as in a Carnot cycle, gives maximum efficiency.

[figure: p4-fig2]

For a reversible engine between two reservoirs, $q_H=w+q_C$ and $q_H/T_H=q_C/T_C$.

parts.statement: What should be the hot-reservoir temperature TH of a Carnot engine to maintain the fuel-cell efficiency calculated in 4.6 if cold-reservoir TC is 40 °C? (If unable to calculate the efficiency, use 0.80.)

figures.alt: Native fuel cell with full H₂/O₂/H₂O labels, electrodes/electrolyte, electron/proton directions and electrical circuit.
Native Carnot-engine reservoirs TH/TC and complete qH/qC/work arrows.

solution.statement:
**4.1**

$$n(\mathrm{H_2})=\frac{0.100\,\mathrm{dm^3\,min^{-1}}\times101.325\,\mathrm{kPa}}{8.314\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}\times298\,\mathrm K}=4.1\cdot10^{-3}\,\mathrm{mol\,min^{-1}}.$$

$$n(\mathrm{Ru})=\frac{4.1\cdot10^{-3}\,\mathrm{mol\,H_2\,min^{-1}}}{92\,\mathrm{mol\,H_2\,min^{-1}}/(1\,\mathrm{mol\,Ru})}=4.5\cdot10^{-5}\,\mathrm{mol}.$$

$m(\mathrm{Ru})=4.5\cdot10^{-5}\times101.07=4.5\cdot10^{-3}\,\mathrm g=4.5\,\mathrm{mg}$.

**4.2** $n(\mathrm{NaBH_4})=1.0\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}\times0.100\,\mathrm{dm^3}=0.10\,\mathrm{mol}$. The key prints “0.04 mol of H₂ are released from 0.10 mol NaBH₄”, followed by:

$$t=\frac{0.40\,\mathrm{mol\,H_2}}{4.1\cdot10^{-3}\,\mathrm{mol\,H_2\,min^{-1}}}=98\,\mathrm{min}.$$

Source note: The prose 0.04 and numerator 0.40 are both printed; neither is silently replaced.

**4.3** $\mathrm{Rate}=k[\mathrm{Ru}]=Ae^{-E_a/(RT)}[\mathrm{Ru}]$.

$$\frac{e^{-E_a/(R\times298)}}{e^{-E_a/(RT)}}=\frac12,\quad-\frac{E_a}{R}\left(\frac1{298}-\frac1T\right)=\ln\frac12.$$

$$\frac{4.20\cdot10^4\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}}{8.314\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}}\left(\frac1{298}-\frac1T\right)=\ln2.$$

T = 311 K or 38 °C.

**4.4** Since $\Delta G^\circ=-nFE^\circ$, $2(-2.37\cdot10^5)=-4\times96485\times E^\circ_{\rm cell}$; $E^\circ_{\rm cell}=1.23\,\mathrm V$. $1.23=E^\circ_{\rm cathode}-(-0.83)$; $E^\circ_{\rm cathode}=0.40\,\mathrm V$.

**4.5** $2.5\,\mathrm A\times3\times3600\,\mathrm s=27000\,\mathrm C$.

$$n(\mathrm{O_2})=27000\,\mathrm C\times\frac{1\,\mathrm{mol}}{4\times96485\,\mathrm C}=0.070\,\mathrm{mol},\quad V(\mathrm{O_2})=\frac{0.070\times8.314\times298}{101.325}=1.7\,\mathrm{dm^3}.$$

V(air) = 8.6 dm³.

**4.6** $\Delta_{\rm rxn}G^\circ=\Delta_{\rm rxn}H^\circ-T\Delta_{\rm rxn}S^\circ$.

$$\Delta_{\rm rxn}S^\circ=2S^\circ(\mathrm{H_2O}(l))-[2S^\circ(\mathrm{H_2}(g))+S^\circ(\mathrm{O_2}(g))]=2\times70.0-(2\times130.7+205.2)=-326.6\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}.$$

$$\Delta_{\rm rxn}H^\circ=\Delta_{\rm rxn}G^\circ+T\Delta_{\rm rxn}S^\circ=-474+298.15(-326.6\cdot10^{-3})=-571.4\,\mathrm{kJ}.$$

Maximum $w=\Delta_{\rm rxn}G^\circ=-474\,\mathrm{kJ}$; $\eta=(-474000\,\mathrm J)/(-571400\,\mathrm J)=0.83$.

**4.7** $\eta_{\rm engine}=w/q_H=(q_H-q_C)/q_H=1-q_C/q_H$. Since $q_H/T_H=q_C/T_C$, $q_C/q_H=T_C/T_H$.

$$\eta_{\rm engine}=1-\frac{T_C}{T_H},\quad0.83=1-\frac{313}{T_H},\quad T_H=1.8\cdot10^3\,\mathrm K\ \text{or}\ T_H\approx1.5\cdot10^3\,{}^\circ\mathrm C.$$

problems.title: Theoretical problem 5 — Polynitrogen compounds
problems.statement: Polynitrogen compounds have great potential for being used as high energy density materials. They are thermodynamically unstable. Huge amount of energy is released from their decomposition or reactions leading to more stable products. The only known polynitrogen species are N₂, N₃⁻ and N₅⁺, isolated in 1772, 1890 and 1999, respectively, and recently reported cyclic anion N₅⁻.

parts.statement: Write the Lewis structure for N₅⁺ with three energetically favourable resonance forms. Indicate the lone pairs and formal charges. Draw the molecular geometry of N₅⁺.
Write the Lewis structures for cyclic N₅⁻ with five energetically favourable resonance forms. Indicate the lone pairs and formal charges. Draw the molecular geometry of cyclic N₅⁻.
The synthesis of [N₅⁺][AsF₆⁻], a white ionic solid, was achieved by reacting [N₂F⁺][AsF₆⁻] with hydrazoic acid HN₃ in liquid HF at −78 °C. Write the balanced chemical equation.
parts.statementAfter:
The preparation of [N₂F⁺][AsF₆⁻] requires reaction of N₂F₂ with strong Lewis acid AsF₅:

x C(graphite) + AsF₅ → Cₓ·AsF₅ (graphite intercalate with x = 10–12),

2 Cₓ·AsF₅ + N₂F₄ → 2 [Cₓ⁺][AsF₆⁻] + trans-N₂F₂,

trans-N₂F₂ + AsF₅ → [N₂F⁺][AsF₆⁻].

In the synthesis of N₂F₂, the trans isomer is formed, which is thermodynamically less stable than cis-N₂F₂. Conversion to cis requires surmounting a high energy barrier of 251 kJ mol⁻¹, so equilibration does not significantly take place without a suitable catalyst. When trans-N₂F₂ is maintained in a closed container for six days at room temperature with a small amount of SbF₅ catalyst, cis-trans thermal equilibrium is established: trans-N₂F₂ ⇌ cis-N₂F₂ at 25 °C. Standard formation enthalpies of trans and cis are 67.31 and 62.03 kJ mol⁻¹; standard entropies at 25 °C are 262.10 and 266.50 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, respectively.

parts.statement: Find the ratio of the number of cis-N₂F₂ molecules over that of trans-N₂F₂ molecules in an equilibrium mixture at 25 °C.

Write the Lewis structures showing geometry of N₂F⁺ ion and trans- and cis-isomers of N₂F₂. Include all lone pairs and formal charges. Suggest an appropriate hybridization for each nitrogen atom in N₂F₂ and N₂F⁺.
parts.statementAfter: Solid [N₅⁺][AsF₆⁻] is marginally stable at room temperature but reacts explosively with water to produce arsenic pentafluoride, hydrogen fluoride, molecular nitrogen and oxygen.

parts.statement: Write a balanced equation for the reaction between [N₅⁺][AsF₆⁻] and water.
parts.statementAfter:
Conversion of [N₅⁺][SbF₆⁻] into other N₅⁺ salts can be achieved by metathesis:

[N₅⁺][SbF₆⁻] + [M⁺][X⁻] → [N₅⁺][X⁻] + [M⁺][SbF₆⁻],

where M⁺ = Na⁺, K⁺, Cs⁺ and X⁻ = a large anion such as SnF₆²⁻ and B(CF₃)₄⁻. Since [Cs⁺][SbF₆⁻] has low solubility in anhydrous HF, and [K⁺][SbF₆⁻] has low solubility in SO₂, these solvents were used extensively for metathesis at −78 °C and −64 °C, respectively.

parts.statement: Write the balanced equations for preparation of [N₅⁺]₂[SnF₆²⁻] and [N₅⁺][B(CF₃)₄⁻] in solution starting with [Cs⁺]₂[SnF₆²⁻] and [K⁺][B(CF₃)₄⁻], respectively. Indicate the appropriate solvent.
parts.statementAfter: When [N₅⁺]₂[SnF₆²⁻] decomposes under carefully controlled conditions at 25–30 °C, [N₅⁺][SnF₅⁻] and N₅F are formed. [N₅⁺][SnF₅⁻] is a white solid with thermal stability comparable to [N₅⁺][SbF₆⁻] (50–60 °C). The solution ¹¹⁹Sn NMR spectrum shows that SnF₅⁻ is a mixture of dimeric and tetrameric polyanions. In both, the coordination number of Sn is 6 and there are bridging fluorine atoms.

parts.statement: Draw the structures of dimeric and tetrameric polyanions.

solution.statement:
**5.1** Formula N₅⁺. The three native Lewis resonance forms, lone pairs/formal charges and bent molecular geometry are:

[figure: p5-sol-fig1]

**5.2** The native heading prints “Cyclic N₅⁺”; its five negative resonance structures and pentagonal molecular geometry are:

[figure: p5-sol-fig2]

Source note: The printed positive heading conflicts with the N₅⁻ question and drawn negative structures; both are preserved.

**5.3** [N₂F⁺][AsF₆⁻] + HN₃ → [N₅⁺][AsF₆⁻] + HF, at −78 °C in HF(l).

**5.4** The desired ratio is the equilibrium constant K for trans ⇌ cis:

$$K=\frac{[\mathrm{cis}]}{[\mathrm{trans}]},\quad\Delta G^\circ=-RT\ln K,\quad\Delta G^\circ=\Delta H^\circ-T\Delta S^\circ.$$

$$\Delta H^\circ=62.03-67.31=-5.28\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}},\quad\Delta S^\circ=266.50-262.10=4.40\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}.$$

$$\Delta G^\circ=-5.28\cdot10^3-(298\times4.40)=-6.59\cdot10^3\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}.$$

$$K=e^{-\Delta G^\circ/(RT)}=e^{-(-6.59\cdot10^3)/(8.314\times298)}=14.3.$$

Thus [cis]/[trans] = 14.3 at 25 °C.

**5.5** The native trans-N₂F₂, cis-N₂F₂ and N₂F⁺ structures, including all lone pairs, formal charges and hybridizations sp²/sp, are:

[figure: p5-sol-fig3]

**5.6** 4 [N₅⁺][AsF₆⁻] + 2 H₂O → 4 AsF₅ + 4 HF + 10 N₂ + O₂.

**5.7** The key prints:

2 [N₅⁺][AsF₆⁻] + Cs₂SnF₆ → [N₅⁺]₂[SnF₆²⁻] + 2 CsSbF₆, in HF at −78 °C;

[N₅⁺][SbF₆⁻] + K⁺[B(CF₃)₄⁻] → [N₅⁺][B(CF₃)₄⁻] + 2 KSbF₆, in SO₂ at −64 °C.

Source note: The first equation has an As/Sb mismatch; the second prints the product coefficient 2. Both printed equations are retained without silent correction.

**5.8** Native dimer Sn₂F₁₀²⁻ and tetramer Sn₄F₂₀⁴⁻, with all terminal and bridging fluorines and bond orientations:

[figure: p5-sol-fig4]

problems.title: Theoretical problem 6 — Thiosulfate leaching of gold
problems.statement:
Extraction of gold using sodium cyanide, a very poisonous chemical, causes environmental problems and serious public concern about the “cyanide process”. Thiosulfate leaching is an alternative. The main reagent, ammonium thiosulfate (NH₄)₂S₂O₃, is relatively non-toxic. Although environmentally benign, the chemistry is complex and needs thorough study. The leaching solution contains S₂O₃²⁻, Cu²⁺, NH₃ and dissolved O₂, and must have pH greater than 8.5 for free ammonia.

The proposed mechanism forms a local voltaic micro-cell on gold particles:

**Anode:**

Au(s) + 2 NH₃(aq) → [Au(NH₃)₂]⁺(aq) + e⁻;

[Au(NH₃)₂]⁺(aq) + 2 S₂O₃²⁻(aq) → [Au(S₂O₃)₂]³⁻(aq) + 2 NH₃(aq).

**Cathode:**

[Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺(aq) + e⁻ → [Cu(NH₃)₂]⁺(aq) + 2 NH₃(aq);

[Cu(NH₃)₂]⁺(aq) + 3 S₂O₃²⁻(aq) → [Cu(S₂O₃)₃]⁵⁻(aq) + 2 NH₃(aq).

parts.statement: Write the overall cell reaction for this voltaic cell.
In the presence of ammonia [Cu(S₂O₃)₃]⁵⁻ is oxidized by O₂ back to [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺. Write a balanced equation for this oxidation-reduction in basic solution.
In this leaching process [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺ functions as a catalyst and speeds dissolution of gold. Write the net overall oxidation-reduction reaction for dissolution of gold metal catalyzed by this ion.
Draw the coordination geometries of the metal in [Au(NH₃)₂]⁺ and [Au(S₂O₃)₂]³⁻, indicating the coordinating atoms.
parts.statementAfter: Their formation constants Kf are 1.00·10²⁶ and 1.00·10²⁸, respectively. Consider equilibrium concentrations [S₂O₃²⁻] = 0.100; [NH₃] = 0.100 and total concentration of gold(I) species = 5.50·10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³.

parts.statement: Calculate the percentage of gold(I) existing as thiosulfate complex.
parts.statementAfter:
When O₂ concentration is not high enough and pH > 10, S₂O₃²⁻ reduces [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺ to [Cu(S₂O₃)₃]⁵⁻ with tetrathionate S₄O₆²⁻ formation:

2 [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺(aq) + 8 S₂O₃²⁻(aq) → 2 [Cu(S₂O₃)₃]⁵⁻(aq) + S₄O₆²⁻(aq) + 8 NH₃(aq).

In basic solution tetrathionate disproportionates to trithionate S₃O₆²⁻ and thiosulfate.

parts.statement: Write a balanced equation for this disproportionation reaction.
When O₂ concentration is too high, S₂O₃²⁻ is oxidized by oxygen to yield trithionate and sulfate ions. Write a balanced equation.

solution.statement:
**6.1** Net anode half reaction:

Au(s) + 2 S₂O₃²⁻(aq) → [Au(S₂O₃)₂]³⁻(aq) + e⁻.

Net cathode half reaction:

[Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺(aq) + 3 S₂O₃²⁻(aq) + e⁻ → [Cu(S₂O₃)₃]⁵⁻(aq) + 4 NH₃(aq).

Overall cell reaction (native heading “erall cell reaction”):

Au(s) + [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺(aq) + 5 S₂O₃²⁻(aq) → [Au(S₂O₃)₂]³⁻(aq) + [Cu(S₂O₃)₃]⁵⁻(aq) + 4 NH₃(aq).

**6.2** Oxidation half reaction:

[Cu(S₂O₃)₃]⁵⁻(aq) + 4 NH₃(aq) → [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺(aq) + 3 S₂O₃²⁻(aq) + e⁻.

Reduction half reaction: O₂(g) + 2 H₂O(l) + 4 e⁻ → 4 OH⁻(aq).

Redox reaction:

4 [Cu(S₂O₃)₃]⁵⁻(aq) + 16 NH₃(aq) + O₂(g) + 2 H₂O(l) → 4 [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺(aq) + 12 S₂O₃²⁻(aq) + 4 OH⁻(aq).

**6.3** Sum the equations:

Au(s) + [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺(aq) + 5 S₂O₃²⁻(aq) → [Au(S₂O₃)₂]³⁻(aq) + [Cu(S₂O₃)₃]⁵⁻(aq) + 4 NH₃(aq);

4 [Cu(S₂O₃)₃]⁵⁻(aq) + 16 NH₃(aq) + O₂(g) + 2 H₂O(l) → 4 [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺(aq) + 12 S₂O₃²⁻(aq) + 4 OH⁻(aq).

Summarizing:

4 Au(s) + 8 S₂O₃²⁻(aq) + O₂(g) + 2 H₂O(l) → 4 [Au(S₂O₃)₂]³⁻(aq) + 4 OH⁻(aq).

**6.4** Coordination geometry: [H₃N–Au–NH₃]⁺ and [O₃S–S–Au–S–SO₃]³⁻, as the native straight-line drawings indicate.

**6.5** Au⁺(aq) + 2 NH₃(aq) → [Au(NH₃)₂]⁺(aq), Kf,1 = 1.00·10²⁶.

Au⁺(aq) + 2 S₂O₃²⁻(aq) → [Au(S₂O₃)₂]³⁻(aq), Kf,2 = 1.00·10²⁸.

Thus [Au(NH₃)₂]⁺(aq) + 2 S₂O₃²⁻(aq) → [Au(S₂O₃)₂]³⁻(aq) + 2 NH₃(aq), with Keq = Kf,2/Kf,1 = 1.00·10².

$$[\mathrm{Au(NH_3)_2^+}]+[\mathrm{Au(S_2O_3)_2^{3-}}]=5.50\cdot10^{-5}\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}.$$

$$K_{\rm eq}=\frac{(0.100)^2x}{(5.50\cdot10^{-5}-x)(0.100)^2}=1.00\cdot10^2,\quad x=5.445\cdot10^{-5}.$$

$$\frac{5.445\cdot10^{-5}}{5.50\cdot10^{-5}}\times100=99.0\%.$$

Thus 99.0% of Au(I) is [Au(S₂O₃)₂]³⁻.

**6.6** S₄O₆²⁻(aq) + 2 e⁻ → 2 S₂O₃²⁻(aq);

12 OH⁻(aq) + 3 S₄O₆²⁻(aq) → 4 S₃O₆²⁻(aq) + 6 H₂O(l) + 10 e⁻.

Disproportionation:

4 S₄O₆²⁻(aq) + 6 OH⁻(aq) → 5 S₂O₃²⁻(aq) + 2 S₃O₆²⁻(aq) + 3 H₂O(l).

**6.7** 2 S₂O₃²⁻(aq) + 2 O₂(g) → SO₄²⁻(aq) + S₃O₆²⁻(aq).

problems.title: Theoretical problem 7 — Synthesis of a carbasugar
problems.statement:
Carbohydrates are essential components of living cells and a source of energy for animals. They include simple sugars with small molecules as well as macromolecular substances. When ring (endocyclic) oxygen in sugars is replaced by methylene, the compounds formed are pseudosugars or carbasugars. Since they are hydrolytically stable towards acids and enzymes, several have found application in glycosidase inhibition. Total syntheses of two isomeric carbasugars with skeleton 1 are described below.

[figure: p7-fig1]

Total synthesis of 1 starts by reduction of benzene by sodium in liquid ammonia to A. The C-13 NMR spectrum of A has two signals at 124.0 and 26.0 ppm. Trichloroacetyl chloride with Zn gives reactive S (Scheme7.1). One equivalent of S undergoes [2+2] cycloaddition with A to racemic B. Reaction of B with Zn in acetic acid gives C, containing only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. C has three sp² carbon signals at 210.0, 126.5 and 125.3 ppm. Reaction of C with one equivalent of m-chloroperbenzoic acid (m-CPBA) in methylene chloride gives D as major product, with three sp²-region C-13 NMR signals at 177.0, 125.8 and 124.0 ppm.

[figure: p7-fig2]

¹³C-NMR chemical shift ranges of typical functional groups.

[figure: p7-fig3]

Scheme7.1.

parts.statementAfter:

Reaction of H with singlet oxygen generated in situ affords I. Although two isomers are theoretically possible, I is formed singly due to steric hindrance and electronic repulsion. Excess LiAlH₄ reduces I to J (Scheme7.3). J shows eight C-13 NMR signals, two sp². Excess acetyl chloride/pyridine gives K from J. OsO₄/4-methylmorpholine4-oxide (NMO) gives stereoisomers L and M. Reduction with excess LiAlH₄ gives 1a and 1b, respectively.

problems.title: Theoretical problem 8 — Click chemistry
problems.statement:
Click chemistry was introduced by K.B.Sharpless in 2001 and describes reactions generating substances quickly, reliably and quantitatively by joining molecules through small units under mild conditions. This methodology has recently been applied as a key step in the synthesis of bicyclic compounds below. Mandelic acid is a versatile natural compound widely used as a “chiral pool”. Reduction of (R)-mandelic acid with LiBH₄ affords A.

[figure: p8-fig1]

Reaction of A with one equivalent of p-toluenesulfonyl chloride gives B (Scheme8.1). Heating B in pyridine yields C; B and C retain their absolute configurations.

[figure: p8-fig2]

Scheme8.1 and native TsCl definition.

parts.statement: Draw structures of B and C with correct stereochemistry. Use dashed-wedged line notation throughout this problem.
parts.statementAfter:
Reaction of C with sodium azide in aqueous acetonitrile gives enantiopure regioisomers D and E in a 3:1 ratio (Scheme8.2). B affords E as sole product under the same condition.
